text: s. The use of dornase alfa has been associated with some improvement in lung function and it might be a use- ful adjunct to bronchial drainage, although it is unclear whether it prevents the development of progressive lung damage. However, a randomised, multicentre, placebo- controlled study in children showed that dornase alfa maintained lung function and reduced the risk of exacerba- tions over a period of 96 weeks.11 Mucolytics such as acet- ylcysteine are generally not considered to be effective in cystic fibrosis.12 Inhalation of hypertonic saline has, how- ever, been shown to be of benefit (see p.1687) and has be- come part of management in many centres.8,9 The time re- quired for such therapies and their associated monitoring may prove challenging to patients and their families.8 In young patients with early disease, prevention or erad- ication of infection for as long as possible is a reasonable aim, in order to maintain good lung function.9 Staphylo- coccal infections commonly develop during the first dec- ade of life, and some clinicians start antistaphylococcal an- tibacterials on diagnosis of cystic fibrosis. Others wait until the first clinical infection occurs before starting treat- ment. Once started, antistaphylococcal therapy is contin- ued indefinitely in some centres, while others only treat when symptomatic exacerbations or positive sputum cul- tures occur. Systematic reviews confirmed that antistaphy- lococcal treatment is effective and also concluded that prophylaxis is likely to be beneficial in young children with cystic fibrosis.13,14 In the UK, flucloxacillin or co- amoxiclav are commonly given.9 It is unclear whether in- termittent or continuous therapy produces the best clinical outcome. Other potential disadvantages to prophylaxis are the possible early acquisition of Ps. aeruginosa infection15 (this seems to be a risk mainly if broad spectrum cepha- losporins are given) and an increased incidence of drug- resistant staphylococci with continuous therapy.16 Management of chronic infection is aimed at control of bacterial load,9 since permanent eradication is impossible. Selection of an antibacterial must be individualised, and will depend on the infecting organisms,9 and local pre- scribing policies and availability. Long-term intermittent treatment with inhaled antibacterials, particularly to- bramycin, is favoured;8,9,17,18 other nebulised antibacteri- als that may be of benefit include aztreonam and colis- tin.8,19 A systematic review confirmed that inhaled antipseudomonal antibacterials improved lung function and reduced the frequency of exacerbations.20 Although there is some evidence of an increase in resistance with such treatment,20 it is claimed to be less frequent than feared.8 In contrast, oral antipseudomonal therapy has not been
